analysis.one_liner: Requires big outside political spenders to name their donors.
analysis.headline: Senate Republicans blocked the campaign-donor disclosure bill from ever reaching the floor; a second vote to advance it fell 7 short, 53-45, with no Republican in favor.
analysis.plain_summary: The DISCLOSE Act would have required corporations, labor unions, Super PACs, and tax-exempt groups that spend more than $10,000 on political ads to file a report within 24 hours, naming any donor who gave $10,000 or more. It would also have expanded the window during which political ads count as campaign spending, and applied the disclosure rules to Super PACs that take unlimited contributions. The bill never came up for a real debate: two procedural votes to start considering it fell short of the 60 needed, and the majority leader then withdrew the motion.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would learn within a day which companies, unions, and wealthy donors were paying for the political ads aimed at them. Candidates and party committees, who would see who was bankrolling outside attacks supporting or opposing them. Ordinary people who give to advocacy groups would still be shielded below the $10,000 threshold.

how_it_helps.text: Requires any corporation, labor organization, tax-exempt 501(c) group, or 527 political organization that spends more than $10,000 on campaign ads or related transfers to file a statement under penalty of perjury within 24 hours, listing each disbursement over $1,000 and every person who gave $10,000 or more [S2][S3].
Extends disclosure rules to Super PACs — political committees with accounts accepting donations that do not comply with federal contribution limits — for those accounts [S3].

Broadens the definition of an independent expenditure to cover the functional equivalent of express advocacy, and stretches the 'electioneering communication' window so ads run starting January 1 of an election year count, not just ads in the final weeks [S2][S3].
Repeals the existing ban on political contributions by individuals age 17 or younger [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Super PACs, tax-exempt 'dark money' organizations, corporations, and labor unions that spend heavily on elections would lose the ability to fund political advertising anonymously. Their donors above $10,000 would be named in public filings within 24 hours.

drawbacks.text: Disclosure names donors, and critics argued this could expose and deter people who give to controversial advocacy groups — the same objection that united many nonprofit groups against the 2010 House version of the bill (widely reported; not in the provided sources).

The rules reach labor organizations and 501(c) nonprofits as well as corporations, and groups spending just over $10,000 must file under penalty of perjury, a compliance burden that weighs most heavily on smaller advocacy organizations [S3].

The repeal of the ban on contributions by 17-year-olds is unrelated to the disclosure regime and was added despite its absence from the 2010 House bill, which critics could read as a donor carve-out (the repeal appears in the CRS summary and bill text; the political interpretation is widely reported).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: voters learn who is funding campaign ads, and big spenders lose anonymity. The $10,000 donor threshold shields most individual givers from exposure while capturing institutional money, and applying the rules equally to unions, corporations, and tax-exempt groups is even-handed. The main honest cost is a compliance and privacy burden on advocacy organizations and their donors, and the bill carries an unrelated 17-year-old contribution repeal that has nothing to do with disclosure. On balance the disclosure benefits are large and the costs manageable.

outcome.mechanism: Two procedural votes to start debating the bill needed 60 senators and failed — 51-44 on July 16, then 53-45 the next day — with every Republican voting no, so the bill was never debated or voted on and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on July 10, 2012, with 28 original Senate cosponsors; it was placed on the Senate calendar two days later [S1][S3][S5].
A first cloture vote on the motion to proceed failed 51-44, with 49 of 51 Democrats in favor and 43 of 47 Republicans opposed [S6].
After the motion to reconsider passed by unanimous consent, a second cloture vote failed 53-45 — every Democrat, Sen. Sanders, and Sen. Lieberman in favor, every Republican opposed [S7].
Majority Leader Reid then withdrew the motion to proceed, and the bill received no floor debate or vote [S5].
The Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution held a hearing on July 24, 2012, but no further action followed before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations, Super PACs, and tax-exempt groups that spend on elections kept the ability to fund political advertising without naming their donors, since the bill died without a floor vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Anonymous campaign spenders and their donors

industries.industry: Super PACs and 'dark money' tax-exempt groups
industries.note: These organizations raise unlimited, often anonymous money for campaign ads, and the bill would have forced them to name donors of $10,000 or more within 24 hours. Their core interest — anonymity — runs directly against voters' interest in knowing who pays for the ads they see.

Corporate political spending would have become public, with the CEO certifying under penalty of perjury that spending was not coordinated with candidates. Corporate political operations have generally opposed disclosure mandates.

Unions are covered by the same disclosure requirements as corporations, and would have had to report spending and large donors. The even-handed coverage is a fairness point, but unions also lost anonymity for their political operations.
